paragraphs: We have now said enough about the effects of Union on the commercial prosperity of the States. Our present inquiry concerns its tendency to promote the interests of revenue.

All enlightened statesmen now see and acknowledge that the prosperity of commerce is the most useful as well as the most productive source of national wealth, and it has accordingly become a primary object of their political care. By multiplying the means of gratification, and by promoting the introduction and circulation of the precious metals, those darling objects of human greed and enterprise, commerce brings new life and vigor to the channels of industry and makes them flow with greater activity and abundance. The diligent merchant, the hardworking farmer, the active mechanic and the industrious manufacturer, all orders of men, look forward with eager expectation and growing readiness to this pleasing reward of their toils. The often-debated question between agriculture and commerce has been settled by indisputable experience. The verdict has silenced the rivalry that once existed between them and has proved, to the satisfaction of their friends, that their interests are closely blended and interwoven. It has been found in various countries that land has risen in value in proportion as commerce has flourished. And how could it have happened otherwise? Could that which gives the products of the earth a freer outlet, which furnishes new incentives to the cultivation of land, which is the most powerful instrument for increasing the quantity of money in a state, could that, in short, which is the faithful handmaid of labor and industry in every form, fail to increase the thing that is the fruitful parent of by far the greatest part of the objects on which labor and industry are exerted? It is astonishing that so simple a truth should ever have had an opponent. It is one proof among a multitude of how readily a spirit of ill-informed jealousy, or of too much abstraction and refinement, leads men away from the plainest truths of reason and conviction.

The ability of a country to pay taxes must always be proportioned, in great degree, to the quantity of money in circulation and to the speed with which it circulates. Commerce contributes to both, and so must of necessity make the payment of taxes easier and make it easier to supply the treasury. The hereditary dominions of the Emperor of Germany contain a great extent of fertile, cultivated and populous territory, a large part of it in mild and luxuriant climates. In some parts of this territory are found the best gold and silver mines in Europe. And yet, for want of the nourishing influence of commerce, that monarch can boast only slender revenues. Several times he has been compelled to depend on the financial aid of other nations to preserve his essential interests, and he cannot sustain a long or continued war on the strength of his own resources.

But this is not the only respect in which Union will be seen to serve the purpose of revenue. There are other points of view in which its influence will appear more immediate and decisive. It is evident from the state of the country, from the habits of the people and from our experience on this very point that it is impracticable to raise any very considerable sums by direct taxation. Tax laws have been multiplied in vain. New methods of enforcing collection have been tried in vain. Public expectation has been disappointed every time, and the treasuries of the States have remained empty. The popular system of administration inherent in the nature of popular government, combined with the real scarcity of money that comes from a languid and crippled state of trade, has so far defeated every attempt at extensive collections, and has at length taught the different legislatures the folly of attempting them.

No one acquainted with what happens in other countries will be surprised at this. In so wealthy a nation as Britain, where direct taxes, because of her greater wealth, must be much easier to bear and, because of the vigor of her government, much more practicable than in America, by far the greatest part of the national revenue comes from taxes of the indirect kind, from imposts and from excises. Duties on imported articles form a large branch of the latter description.

In America it is evident that for a long time we must depend chiefly on such duties for our revenue. In most parts of the country excises must be confined within a narrow compass. The character of the people will ill endure the prying and peremptory spirit of excise laws. The farmers, on the other hand, will yield only scanty supplies, and reluctantly, in the unwelcome form of impositions on their houses and lands. And personal property is too uncertain and invisible a fund to be reached in any way other than by the imperceptible operation of taxes on consumption.

If these remarks have any foundation, then the state of things that will best enable us to improve and extend so valuable a resource must be best suited to our political welfare. And it cannot admit of serious doubt that this state of things must rest on the basis of a general Union. To the extent that Union would serve the interests of commerce, it must tend to extend the revenue to be drawn from that source. To the extent that it would help make the regulations for collecting the duties simpler and more effective, it must serve to make the same rate of duties more productive and to put it in the power of the government to raise the rate without harm to trade.

The relative situation of these States, the number of rivers that cross them and of bays that wash their shores, the ease of communication in every direction, the likeness of language and manners and the familiar habits of intercourse: all these circumstances would combine to make illicit trade between them a matter of little difficulty, and would ensure frequent evasions of each other's commercial regulations. Mutual jealousy would force the separate States or confederacies to avoid the temptations to that kind of trade by keeping their duties low. For a long time to come, the temper of our governments would not permit those rigorous precautions by which the European nations guard the approaches into their respective countries, by land as well as by water, and which even there are found to be insufficient obstacles to the adventurous stratagems of greed.

In France an army of patrols, as they are called, is constantly employed to protect their fiscal regulations against the inroads of smugglers. Mr. Neckar puts the number of these patrols at upwards of twenty thousand. This shows the immense difficulty of preventing that kind of traffic where there is communication by land, and it puts in a strong light the disadvantages with which the collection of duties in this country would be burdened if disunion should place the States in a situation toward each other resembling that of France toward her neighbors. The arbitrary and vexatious powers with which the patrols are necessarily armed would be intolerable in a free country.

If, on the contrary, there is but one government pervading all the States, then for the principal part of our commerce there will be but ONE SIDE to guard, the ATLANTIC COAST. Vessels arriving directly from foreign countries with valuable cargoes would rarely choose to expose themselves to the complicated and critical perils that would attend attempts to unload before coming into port. They would have to fear both the dangers of the coast and detection, after as well as before their arrival at their final destinations. An ordinary degree of vigilance would be enough to prevent any material violations of the rights of the revenue. A few armed vessels, wisely stationed at the entrances of our ports, might at small expense be made useful sentinels of the laws. And since the government would have the same interest in guarding against violations everywhere, the cooperation of its measures in each State would have a powerful tendency to make them effective. Here also we should preserve through Union an advantage that nature holds out to us and that separation would give up. The United States lie at a great distance from Europe, and at a considerable distance from all other places with which they would have extensive connections of foreign trade. A passage from them to us in a few hours, or in a single night, as between the coasts of France and Britain and of other neighboring nations, would be impracticable. This is a prodigious security against direct smuggling from foreign countries. But smuggling by a roundabout route into one State through another would be both easy and safe. The difference between a direct importation from abroad and an indirect importation through a neighboring State, in small parcels as time and opportunity allow, with the added advantages of communication by land, must be plain to every man of discernment.

It is therefore evident that one national government would be able, at much less expense, to extend the duties on imports incomparably further than would be practicable for the States separately or for any partial confederacies. So far, I believe it may safely be asserted, these duties have not averaged more than three per cent in any State. In France they are estimated at about fifteen per cent, and in Britain they exceed that proportion.(1) There seems to be nothing to prevent their being raised in this country to at least three times their present amount. The single article of ardent spirits, under federal regulation, might be made to yield a considerable revenue. On a ratio to the importation into this State, the whole quantity imported into the United States may be estimated at four million gallons, which at a shilling per gallon would produce two hundred thousand pounds. That article would well bear this rate of duty, and if it should tend to reduce consumption, such an effect would be equally favorable to the agriculture, the economy, the morals and the health of society. There is perhaps nothing that is so much a subject of national extravagance as these spirits.

What will be the consequence if we are not able to take advantage of this resource to its full extent? A nation cannot long exist without revenues. Deprived of this essential support, it must give up its independence and sink into the degraded condition of a province. This is an extremity to which no government will willingly come. Revenue, therefore, must be had at all events. In this country, if the principal part is not drawn from commerce, it must fall with oppressive weight on land. It has already been suggested that excises, in their true sense, are too little in harmony with the feelings of the people to allow great use of that mode of taxation. Nor, indeed, in the States where almost the only occupation is agriculture, are the objects suitable for excise numerous enough to permit very ample collections in that way. Personal estate, as has been remarked before, is too hard to trace to be made to bear large contributions by any means other than taxes on consumption. In populous cities it may be enough a matter of guesswork to cause the oppression of individuals without much total benefit to the State, but beyond these circles it must, in great measure, escape the eye and hand of the tax collector. As the necessities of the State must nevertheless be met in some way, the lack of other resources must throw the principal weight of public burdens on the owners of land. And as, on the other hand, the wants of the government can never be adequately supplied unless all the sources of revenue are open to its demands, the finances of the community under such embarrassments cannot be put in a condition consistent with its respectability or its security. Thus we shall not even have the consolation of a full treasury to make up for the oppression of that valuable class of citizens who are employed in cultivating the soil. But public and private distress will keep pace with each other in gloomy concert, and will unite in lamenting the infatuation of those counsels that led to disunion.
